newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to be specific in State of Union speech.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to be specific in State of Union speech.

text.p: In his State of the Union speech on Tuesday night, President Bill Clinton will draw a map to the "land of new promise" he spoke of grandly at his second inaugural. Aides say it will include many specifics, but no startling new twists or turns.

"I don't think you're going to see a lot of surprises in terms of the president's proposals," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said. "That's exactly what he put before the American people last year" in his re-election campaign.

Clinton, who began a second four-year term as U.S. chief executive on Jan. 20, ran on a platform of balancing the budget by 2002, raising the level of education, moving poor people from welfare to work and keeping the economy strong.

After pushing the limits of ethics and taste in raising money for his re-election push, the Democratic president says he wants to clean up money in politics and will urge the Republican Congress to help him in that endeavour.
"He'll say American democracy at this point, after the troubles of 1996, clearly needs to be reinvigorated with campaign finance reform," McCurry said.

Internationally, Clinton's priorities include nurturing a united, democratic Europe, advancing U.S. interests in the Asian Pacific region, combating trans-national threats like terrorism and drug trafficking and making peace in such hot spots as Bosnia, the Middle East and Northern Ireland.

Keenly aware that history will remember him chiefly as the president who led the United States into the 21st Century, Clinton painted a sunny vision of the outlook for the nation and the world in his inaugural address 12 days ago.

"It is our great good fortune that time and chance have put us not only at the edge of a new century, in a new millenium, but on the edge of a bright new prospect in human affairs, a moment that will define our course and character for decades to come," he said.

Clinton barely mentioned foreign policy in his 22-minute inaugural speech. His State of the Union follow-up will be significantly longer -- possibly an hour or more -- and National Security Adviser Samuel Berger said it will have greater focus on world affairs.

"I would expect the president to outline the fundamental strategic objectives of his second term in both broad terms and with some specifics to chart the course he sees us on over the next four years," he said.

Berger added that Clinton was likely to offer to expand his peacemaking efforts, taking "a more active role in the Aegean, if we can be useful there." NATO allies Greece and Turkey have often come close to war over claims to Aegean islands and over the island of Cyprus.

The speech will fulfil a constitutional mandate which dictates that the president "shall from time to time give to the Congress information of the State of the Union, and recommend to their consideration such measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient."

But Clinton, who rides an approval rating of better than 60 percent in the opinion polls at the moment despite the commotion over Democratic campaign fund-raising tactics, has shown his ability to turn the occasion into political art.

In his kiss n' tell book "Behind the Oval Office," Dick Morris, the former Clinton political consultant caught in a sex scandal involving a prostitute, describes Clinton's 1996 State of the Union address as the defining moment of last year's presidential race.

Morris reveals that every one of Clinton's "values agenda" proposals in last year's speech were carefully poll-tested in advance to ensure they would be well received by the American people. The White House acknowledges this has also been done for Tuesday night's speech -- and makes no apologies for it.
